The minimum area is π/6, so a = 1, b = 6 and 100a + b = 106. I did not rigorously check that no point outside the square has all four angles above 60°; I took that as plausible from a bound on the angle subtended by the far side.

**Setup.** Γ works exactly when it contains every point P with all four angles ∠APB, ∠BPC, ∠CPD, ∠DPA greater than 60°. Points on the boundary of Γ are allowed to have minimum angle exactly 60°.

**Region inside the square.** Take the square as [0,1]² with center O at the origin of shifted coordinates. For a side such as AB, the points on the square's side of AB with ∠APB > 60° lie inside the circle through A and B with inscribed angle 60°. That circle has radius 1/√3, and its center lies at distance 1/(2√3) from AB, toward the inside of the square.

The bad region is the intersection of the four such discs. Each disc center is at distance d = 1/2 − 1/(2√3) = (√3−1)/(2√3) from O.

**Farthest points from O.** The farthest points of the intersection are its vertices, which lie on the diagonals. Take the vertex toward a corner, at (−u, −u). It lies on the boundary of the discs centered at (0, d) and (d, 0), so

u² + (u+d)² = 1/3.

Simplifying gives u² + du − √3/12 = 0. With d² = (2−√3)/6, the discriminant is d² + √3/3 = (2+√3)/6, whose square root is (√3+1)/(2√3). Then

u = (−d + (√3+1)/(2√3))/2 = 1/(2√3).

The vertex distance from O is u√2 = 1/√6 ≈ 0.408. The arc midpoints are closer, at 1/√3 − d ≈ 0.366.

**Region outside the square.** For P outside, say beyond side AB, the angle ∠CPD is at most about 2·arctan(1/2) ≈ 53° < 60°. Corner regions behave similarly, so I took these points to have minimum angle at most 60°. The bad region is therefore the one inside the square.

**Minimal circle.** The bad region is symmetric about O, with four vertices at distance 1/√6 from O. The smallest circle containing it is centered at O with radius 1/√6. Its area is π/6.

ANSWER: 106
